source.title: Internal Data Repetition Destroys Language Models
source.authors: Jessica Chudnovsky; Joshua Kazdan; Noam Levi; Rylan Schaeffer; Yegor Denisov-Blanch; Bo-Yang He; M. Donmez; O. Koyejo; D. Donoho

record.tranche_reason: The study fits a held-out loss-versus-compute power law on newly trained Qwen3-style models, testing the scaling claim in a different model and data setting rather than reproducing the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own no-repetition scaling-law fit and results from repeated-data training sweeps. It also reports a power law for the repeat count and repeated-pool size at peak damage; those outcomes are recorded as findings not covered by the claim versions. Cited scaling-law results from other studies are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own held-out-loss power law in compute (L = E + KC^−γ) to six newly trained no-repetition Qwen3-style baselines on FineWeb-Edu-Dedup. These span about 1.4e17 to 1.4e19 FLOP. This is a V1-relevant result in a new model and data setting. The fit is mainly used as a reference instrument for the repetition study, not aimed at testing scaling laws, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that, at a fixed 10% repeated-token fraction and fixed compute, exact document repetition does the most damage at an intermediate repeat count. The peak location follows a power-law trend in model size: larger models peak at fewer repeats of larger pools. Under their fitted no-repetition law, the 344M worst setting has CEL ≈ 0.33. They add that how often duplicates appear, not just how much data is duplicated, matters. They treat absolute CEL values as point estimates and the non-monotonicity as the robust finding.
record.recipe_differences: Fits a Chinchilla-form loss-versus-compute curve to six no-repetition baselines in a Qwen3-style model family, then uses it to assess repetition damage; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law experiments or their parameter/token allocation sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The overtraining multiplier shifts the level of CEG but reportedly leaves the peak repeat count approximately unchanged. The absolute CEG/CEL values depend on the fitted loss floor; the authors report a 1% shift in (L − E) produces about a 3% relative shift in CEG and say smaller models are more sensitive.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed compute and a 10% repeated-token fraction, held-out loss peaks at an intermediate repeat count: 1.0–4.2% above baseline, median 3.1%. Worst-setting CEL at OT=1 rises from 0.19 at 34M to 0.33 at 344M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Partial exact-document repetition at fixed repeated-token fraction causes a non-monotonic loss penalty in repeat count, and the compute-equivalent cost grows with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: The peak-damage repeat count and repeated-pool size follow power laws in N and C: Rpeak ∝ N^−0.96 and Drpeak ∝ N^1.84.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The most damaging repetition structure scales as a power law in model size and compute.

fits_no_version.finding: A misspecified linear regression with verbatim duplicates reproduces the intermediate-repeat loss peak in closed form and in simulation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intermediate-repeat generalization peaks can arise from duplicated samples in misspecified models.

record.problems: Experiments use one Qwen3-style model family, one tokenizer, one corpus, and a fixed repeated-token fraction. Each completed cell is a single run, so seed-level variance is not estimated. The largest model is 344M parameters and its grid is limited to OT=1. The no-repetition scaling law is fitted to six points, described as being at the boundary of identifiability for its three-parameter form; absolute CEG/CEL values are point estimates. The loss fit does not independently vary parameters, tokens, and compute.

untested.parts: Separate power laws in parameters or in tokens: N and T are tied at 20 tokens/param at OT=1. Ranges beyond about two orders of magnitude in compute. The OT≠1 baselines are not included in any reported loss-scaling fit.
No extrapolation of small-run fits to larger runs.
No iso-FLOP search for the compute-optimal N/T split. Appendix G notes that 20 tokens/param may not be optimal here, but this is not tested.
No loss-vs-scale power-law fit under repeated data or in other modalities. The power laws reported for repeated data describe peak-damage location, not loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or alternative forms. Sensitivity of CEG to the fitted floor E is discussed only for the CEG metric.

record.verdict_notes: I removed the reader's V1 limits_scope label. Its reasons (six points, tied N/T, narrow range) describe parts of V1 that were not tested, so they are listed under untested. The no-repetition fit is a by-product used to convert loss into CEG. It has only six points, a learning rate not tuned per size, and a single seed, so it is weak support. The paper cites Gadre et al. and Porian et al. on extrapolation and fit robustness, but those are cited results, not rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits loss against compute using six OT=1 no-repetition baselines, with model size and token count tied to compute. It does not independently test loss scaling in parameters or tokens, other non-bottleneck regimes, or the claim across several orders of magnitude.
It does not test whether fits on small runs predict substantially larger runs.
It does not search for loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
It does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count to measure effects of depth, width, or other architecture details.

The study varies repetition structure and measures its effect on loss, but does not test whether the same loss scaling-law form holds across scale under repeated-data training or in other modalities and regimes.
It reports held-out pretraining loss, not downstream-task performance or its predictability.

It notes sensitivity and limitations of its fitted reference curve but does not compare exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, setups, or alternative fits, nor test whether scaling curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: six Qwen3-style no-repetition baselines (34M, 48M, 63M, 93M, 153M, and 344M)
rows.operation_detail: Fit held-out evaluation loss against compute using the six OT=1, R=1 no-repetition baselines.
rows.measure: Held-out evaluation loss as a function of training compute
rows.value: L(C) = 2.365 + 6.647 × 10^5 C^−0.317; the fitted curve matches the six baselines to within about 0.015 nats.
rows.uncertainty: The fit is based on six points; the three-parameter form is described as being at the boundary of identifiability.
rows.note: This is a compute-axis fit in one model family and data setting. At OT=1, model size, tokens, and compute are linked rather than varied independently.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. The paper reports the power law matching all six baselines to within about 0.015 nats over roughly two orders of magnitude in compute. The narrow range and the tied N/T axes are untested parts of V1, not a weaker effect. Caveats: the fit has only six points and is 'at the boundary of identifiability'. Peak learning rate was not tuned per model size.

rows.subject: all completed Qwen3-style repetition sweeps

rows.subject: misspecified linear regression with verbatim duplicated samples
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate population test loss as repeated-pool size and repeat count vary, against a clean no-repetition baseline.

conditions.value: 10% of training budget in the sample-efficiency analysis

rows.measure: Excess population test loss and sample-efficiency analogue
rows.baseline: No-repetition baseline at the same m
rows.value: The text reports non-monotonic test loss and sample efficiency, with a peak at intermediate repetition; theory and simulation agree within numerical precision.
rows.note: This is a statistical analogue for repetition damage, not a test of language-model loss scaling.

relationships.condition: Six OT=1, R=1 Qwen3-style baselines (34M–344M) on FineWeb-Edu-Dedup, roughly 1e17–1e19 FLOP
relationships.reason: A saturating power law in compute (γ≈0.317, E≈2.365) fits all six held-out losses within about 0.015 nats (r1). The evidence is weak: six points, two decades of compute, and a fit used as an instrument.
relationships.display_finding: A saturating compute power law with exponent approximately 0.317 and floor 2.365 fits all six held-out losses within about 0.015 nats across two decades.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
